extracted.intended_audience: pipeline operators, pipeline industry associations, state/federal pipeline safety regulators, and other stakeholders for gas and hazardous liquid pipelines
extracted.subtask_description: Evaluation and implementation criteria for rupture-mitigation valves (RMVs) and alternative equivalent technologies on newly constructed or entirely replaced gas and hazardous liquid pipelines, including definitions, applicability, timelines, notification procedures, and valve spacing/location requirements under the PHMSA final rule.

rubrics_metrics.name: RMV definition and eligible technologies
rubrics_metrics.description: PHMSA made explicit that an RMV is an ASV or an RCV. A valve on crossover piping that is locked and tagged closed in accordance with operating procedures would qualify as an alternative equivalent technology. Other suggested technologies (such as check valves) will be considered on a case-by-case, site-specific basis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When determining appropriateness of alternative equivalent technologies for a particular site, PHMSA will consider technical and safety information submitted by an operator including, but not limited to, design, construction, maintenance, and operating procedures; technology design and operating characteristics such as operation times (closure times for manual valves); service reliability and life; accessibility to operator personnel; nearby population density; and potential consequences to the environment and the public.

rubrics_metrics.name: Shut-off segment definition
rubrics_metrics.description: Shut-off segments (relevant when RMVs or alternative equivalent technologies are installed pursuant to this final rule for Class 3 and Class 4 locations for gas pipelines, and HCAs or segments that could affect HCAs for hazardous liquid pipelines) are defined as segments of pipe located between the upstream mainline valve closest to the upstream endpoint of the new or entirely replaced Class 3, Class 4, or HCA segment, and the downstream mainline valve closest to the downstream endpoint of the new or entirely replaced Class 3, Class 4, or HCA segment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Shut-off segments can include crossover or lateral pipe depending on where that pipe connects to the specific shut-off segment. Single shut-off segments can include multiple Class 3, Class 4, or HCA pipeline segments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of 'entirely replaced' pipeline segments
rubrics_metrics.description: PHMSA intends 'entirely replaced' to mean replacement projects where 2 or more miles of pipe have been replaced within any 5 contiguous miles of pipe within any 24-month period.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: PHMSA clarified this to avoid applying RMV/alternative-technology requirements to small maintenance replacements (e.g., road crossings or anomaly repairs). The 2-or-more-miles-in-any-5-contiguous-miles-within-24-months test was adopted to mitigate potential circumvention by scheduling smaller adjacent replacements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Applicability: stress level / PIR / class-location exemptions and limits
rubrics_metrics.description: PHMSA considered but limited exemptions based on operating stress and Potential Impact Radius (PIR). Pipelines operating below 20% SMYS are at lower rupture risk but are not categorically exempt. For natural gas: PHMSA believes it is feasible to exempt pipelines with PIR <= 150 feet if they are in Class 1 or Class 2 locations; PHMSA did not accept a PIR-based exception for Class 3 locations. For hazardous liquid pipelines: low-stress rural pipelines are generally not exempt due to environmental consequences, though regulated rural gathering pipelines are exempt unless they cross bodies of water greater than 100 feet wide. For gathering lines: operators of Type A gas gathering pipelines in Class 2 with PIR <= 150 ft are not required to install RMVs; Type B gathering lines, operating at <20% SMYS, are generally exempt but will be monitored.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: PHMSA noted historical ruptures at low hoop stresses and will monitor data. Exemptions are tied to class location and PIR thresholds and are not blanket exemptions based solely on low operating pressure. The 5 percent volume contribution for laterals is based on total volume (§192.634(b)(3)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Timeframe to make RMVs operational after placing pipeline in service
rubrics_metrics.description: Operators must make RMVs and alternative equivalent technologies operational within 14 days after placing pipelines into service (PHMSA adjusted from a proposed 7 days).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: PHMSA provides a procedural mechanism for operators to request an extension beyond 14 days if completion of necessary activities is not economically, technically, or operationally feasible (e.g., prohibitive costs, labor/component shortages, required permitting or access rights). Requests are processed per §§192.18 and 195.18.

rubrics_metrics.name: Implementation period for RMV/alternative technology installation
rubrics_metrics.description: Pipelines and pipeline segments installed or entirely replaced beginning 12 months after the publication date of the final rule are required to have RMVs or alternative equivalent technologies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: PHMSA concluded 12 months is reasonable for sourcing and planning; operators anticipating inability to meet the timeframe may request additional time under §§192.18 and 195.18, and PHMSA has discretion to grant or deny based on operator-provided information (economic, technical, or operational feasibility).

rubrics_metrics.name: Notification and review process for alternative technologies, methods, compliance timelines, or valve spacing
rubrics_metrics.description: PHMSA aligned gas notifications with §192.18 and created §195.18 for hazardous liquid pipelines. Operators submit pertinent requested information in advance of installation. PHMSA has 90 days to review and respond to the notification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If PHMSA does not issue an objection or request more time within 90 days, the operator may use the alternative technology/method/timeline/spacing requested. PHMSA will provide a formal 'no objection' letter or email to establish a record. An objection will specify reasons for disapproval; a request for more time extends the review period.

rubrics_metrics.name: Valve spacing for new gas pipeline construction (per §192.179(a))
rubrics_metrics.description: For new gas pipeline construction, RMV/alternative equivalent technology spacing will follow existing §192.179(a) class-location-based intervals: Class 4 — 2.5-mile intervals; Class 3 — 4-mile intervals; Class 2 — 7.5-mile intervals; Class 1 — 10-mile intervals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: PHMSA is applying the current class-location spacing methodology for new construction and citing operator practices (one-class bump) in implementation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Valve spacing for gas pipeline replacement projects
rubrics_metrics.description: For replacements, PHMSA allows operators to use the maximum valve spacing of the class below the replacement project's class location. In practice, this yields maximum spacing for replacement projects of: Class 4 → 8 miles; Class 3 → 15 miles; Class 1 and Class 2 → 20 miles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If RMV or alternative equivalent technology spacing exceeds the spacing for the next class location, a new RMV or alternative equivalent technology is required. PHMSA will monitor data in these locations to ensure spacing does not create undue risk.

rubrics_metrics.name: Valve spacing for hazardous liquid pipelines (HCAs and non-HCAs)
rubrics_metrics.description: PHMSA finalized minimum valve spacing standards for hazardous liquid pipeline segments: 15 miles for segments in, or which could affect, HCAs; and 20 miles for segments that could not affect HCAs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: PHMSA's rationale cites industry data (2015–2019) showing an average of 1 valve installed per 7 miles on constructed/replaced hazardous liquid pipeline mileage; PHMSA determined 15/20-mile minimums are not onerous and will monitor outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Valve location considerations at water crossings and floodplain definitions (proposal and stakeholder input)
rubrics_metrics.description: NPRM proposed a maximum 1-mile spacing for pipelines at water crossings >100 feet in width so the valve would be located outside the flood plain, or actuators/controls would be otherwise unaffected by floodwaters. Commenters asked PHMSA to specify 'flood plain' (suggested 100-year flood plain) and to remove or provide alternatives to the 1-mile limitation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Committees recommended specifying the 100-year flood plain for hazardous liquid pipeline water crossings and offered flexibility when a 1-mile limit falls within the flood plain. PHMSA invited clarification and consideration of alternative spacing relief via notification procedures, though the final determination for water-crossing location specifics is addressed within the rulemaking text and related cross-references.

rubrics_metrics.name: Operational block valves, RMV proximity, and termination location clarifications
rubrics_metrics.description: Committee recommendations (adopted as clarifications) specify that: (1) replacement projects in non-HCA Class 1 and Class 2 locations do not require RMVs/alternative technologies unless the replacement involves a valve (the 'opportunistic approach'); (2) a 'shut-off segment' must contain the newly constructed or replaced HCA or Class 3 or Class 4 pipeline segment; (3) RMVs/alternative equivalent technologies would not be required at the downstream termination of a pipeline; and (4) operational block valves are allowed within a shut-off segment and RMVs need not be the nearest valve to a shut-off segment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Operators requested and PHMSA clarified cross-references and rule language to ensure the opportunistic approach is preserved, to avoid creating valve spacing more stringent than current requirements, and to allow operational flexibility within shut-off segments. PHMSA's formal definitions and cross-references implement these clarifications in the final rule text.
